_comment: Which builds of 0G's broker image a provider may run. A build is accepted when its
SLSA provenance, attached to the image in the registry as a Sigstore bundle, verifies
against Sigstore's public-good trust root (fetched over TUF; trusted_root.json is the
fallback snapshot) AND its signing certificate says it came from the release workflow
below, run on a release tag at or above minimum_version, on a GitHub-hosted runner,
triggered by the tag push. Nothing here
changes when the broker ships: a new release is accepted because the release workflow
signed it, not because someone added it to a list.
WHY THE WORKFLOW AND THE TAG REF, NOT JUST THE REPOSITORY. The broker repository signs
builds from two workflows. build.yml runs on a pushed v* tag and attaches SLSA
provenance; docker-publish.yml is run by hand on any branch and signs too. Two broker
builds running on mainnet on 2026-10-16 (sha256:c5126640…, sha256:459345ec…) carry
valid signatures from docker-publish.yml on refs/heads/main. Accepting any signature
from the repository would accept them.
WHY A MINIMUM VERSION. v0.5.1 and v0.5.2 were built and signed by build.yml on their
release tags exactly as v0.5.4 was; their signatures are valid. They predate broker
#759 (the controller may create no container unless the compose enables it) and #763
(ingress no longer holds dstack.sock), which the docker.sock exception rests on. A
signature proves which workflow built a build, not what the build contains, so the
floor is a statement about code and has to be written down.
WHAT THIS STILL TRUSTS. Whoever can push a v* tag to the broker repository can have
build.yml build and sign any commit, including one that edits build.yml; the
certificate records the commit, so that is auditable after the fact but not prevented
here. The broker repository should restrict v* tag creation with a ruleset.
`revoked` lists builds to refuse despite a valid signature, each with the reason. Fields
are compared exactly; minimum_version is vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.
